name: Gideon
charge: Throwing down the altar of Baal in his father's house; going against Midian with three hundred, as the Lord said
summary: Threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites, the least in his father's house was called a mighty man of valour. He cut down Baal's altar by night, sent home thirty-one thousand seven hundred men because the Lord said the army was too big, and broke the Midianites with pitchers, lamps and trumpets.
offense: Before the Lord sent a deliverer, he sent a prophet. Midian had destroyed Israel's increase until the people hid in dens and caves, but the prophet named the cause: the Lord had brought them out of Egypt, and they had not obeyed his voice (Judges 6:1-10). Gideon's question—where were the miracles their fathers had told them of?—stood within that answer (Judges 6:13). The Lord had not lost his power. Israel had departed from him. The angel called Gideon a mighty man of valour while he threshed wheat in a winepress to hide it. Gideon answered with his family's poverty and his own low place, but the Lord answered with his presence (Judges 6:11-16). First Corinthians 1:26-29 shows the same order: God chooses what the world counts weak so that flesh will not glory before him. The commission was not founded upon Gideon's standing among men. His first commanded work was at home. He threw down his father's altar of Baal, cut down the grove, and built an altar to the Lord. Fear made him work by night, but he still did what was commanded (Judges 6:25-27). When the men of the city demanded his death, Joash answered that Baal should plead for himself if he were a god (Judges 6:28-32). An idol whose worshippers must defend it cannot be the deliverer of those worshippers. Before Gideon confronted Midian, he confronted the false worship in his own household. The Lord then reduced the army from thirty-two thousand to ten thousand, and from ten thousand to three hundred (Judges 7:2-7). Gideon had to release men he might naturally have wanted to keep. The reason was given: Israel must not boast that its own hand had saved it. Deuteronomy 8:14-18 had warned against that very pride. Obedience required trusting the Lord's choice even when it made the army look weaker.
judgment: The Lord strengthened Gideon before the attack by sending him with Phurah to hear the enemy's dream and its interpretation. Gideon heard that Midian had been delivered into his hand, worshipped, and returned ready to act (Judges 7:9-15). The one who had asked for assurance was prepared for the work, not excused from it. Three companies sounded trumpets, broke their pitchers, held their lamps, and stood every man in his place. The Lord set the enemy's swords against one another (Judges 7:16-22). Numbers 10:9 connects the alarm of trumpets in war with being remembered before the Lord and saved from the oppressor. The trumpets were joined to that covenant remembrance; victory did not come from noise apart from the God who heard it. Other Israelites joined the pursuit, and Ephraim took Oreb and Zeeb. When Ephraim complained, Gideon answered by acknowledging what God had delivered into their hands, and their anger abated (Judges 7:23-25; 8:1-3). He had to lead brethren as well as defeat an enemy. Midian was subdued and the country rested forty years (Judges 8:28). The victory was the Lord's from the calling of the least man to the scattering of the great host.

verses.text: And there came an angel of the Lord, and sat under an oak which was in Ophrah, that pertained unto Joash the Abi–ezrite: and his son Gideon threshed wheat by the winepress, to hide it from the Midianites.
And the angel of the Lord appeared unto him, and said unto him, The Lord is with thee, thou mighty man of valour.

And Gideon said unto him, Oh my Lord, if the Lord be with us, why then is all this befallen us? and where be all his miracles which our fathers told us of, saying, Did not the Lord bring us up from Egypt? but now the Lord hath forsaken us, and delivered us into the hands of the Midianites.
And the Lord looked upon him, and said, Go in this thy might, and thou shalt save Israel from the hand of the Midianites: have not I sent thee?
And he said unto him, Oh my Lord, wherewith shall I save Israel? behold, my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house.
And the Lord said unto him, Surely I will be with thee, and thou shalt smite the Midianites as one man.

And it came to pass the same night, that the Lord said unto him, Take thy father’s young bullock, even the second bullock of seven years old, and throw down the altar of Baal that thy father hath, and cut down the grove that is by it:

And build an altar unto the Lord thy God upon the top of this rock, in the ordered place, and take the second bullock, and offer a burnt sacrifice with the wood of the grove which thou shalt cut down.

Then Gideon took ten men of his servants, and did as the Lord had said unto him: and so it was, because he feared his father’s household, and the men of the city, that he could not do it by day, that he did it by night.

And when the men of the city arose early in the morning, behold, the altar of Baal was cast down, and the grove was cut down that was by it, and the second bullock was offered upon the altar that was built.
And the Lord said unto Gideon, The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me.

Now therefore go to, proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, Whosoever is fearful and afraid, let him return and depart early from mount Gilead. And there returned of the people twenty and two thousand; and there remained ten thousand.

And the Lord said unto Gideon, The people are yet too many; bring them down unto the water, and I will try them for thee there: and it shall be, that of whom I say unto thee, This shall go with thee, the same shall go with thee; and of whomsoever I say unto thee, This shall not go with thee, the same shall not go.

So he brought down the people unto the water: and the Lord said unto Gideon, Every one that lappeth of the water with his tongue, as a dog lappeth, him shalt thou set by himself; likewise every one that boweth down upon his knees to drink.
And the number of them that lapped, putting their hand to their mouth, were three hundred men: but all the rest of the people bowed down upon their knees to drink water.
And the Lord said unto Gideon, By the three hundred men that lapped will I save you, and deliver the Midianites into thine hand: and let all the other people go every man unto his place.

So the people took victuals in their hand, and their trumpets: and he sent all the rest of Israel every man unto his tent, and retained those three hundred men: and the host of Midian was beneath him in the valley.
And he divided the three hundred men into three companies, and he put a trumpet in every man’s hand, with empty pitchers, and lamps within the pitchers.
And he said unto them, Look on me, and do likewise: and, behold, when I come to the outside of the camp, it shall be that, as I do, so shall ye do.
When I blow with a trumpet, I and all that are with me, then blow ye the trumpets also on every side of all the camp, and say, The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon.

So Gideon, and the hundred men that were with him, came unto the outside of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch; and they had but newly set the watch: and they blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers that were in their hands.

And the three companies blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers, and held the lamps in their left hands, and the trumpets in their right hands to blow withal: and they cried, The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon.
And they stood every man in his place round about the camp: and all the host ran, and cried, and fled.

And the three hundred blew the trumpets, and the Lord set every man’s sword against his fellow, even throughout all the host: and the host fled to Beth–shittah in Zererath, and to the border of Abel–meholah, unto Tabbath.
Thus was Midian subdued before the children of Israel, so that they lifted up their heads no more. And the country was in quietness forty years in the days of Gideon.
And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets:
Who through faith subdued kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions,
Quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.

When thou goest out to battle against thine enemies, and seest horses, and chariots, and a people more than thou, be not afraid of them: for the Lord thy God is with thee, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.
And it shall be, when ye are come nigh unto the battle, that the priest shall approach and speak unto the people,
And shall say unto them, Hear, O Israel, ye approach this day unto battle against your enemies: let not your hearts faint, fear not, and do not tremble, neither be ye terrified because of them;
For the Lord your God is he that goeth with you, to fight for you against your enemies, to save you.

entries.commentary: Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord delivered them into the hand of Midian seven years. That is our manner: the Most High delivers us, we get a little bit of freedom, and we go right back to wickedness. The same thing goes on today; we get relaxed, and the Lord has to remind us, putting us right back into hard bondage, that this is not our rest. Because of the Midianites, the children of Israel made them the dens in the mountains, and caves, and strongholds; Israel hid in the mountains of their own land.

When Israel had sown, the Midianites, the Amalekites, and the children of the east came up as grasshoppers for multitude, destroyed the increase of the earth, and left no sustenance for Israel, neither sheep, nor ox, nor ass, and Israel was greatly impoverished. That goes right into the curses.

When Israel cried unto the Lord, the Lord sent a prophet to remind them: I brought you up from Egypt out of the house of bondage, and I said, fear not the gods of the Amorites in whose land ye dwell, but ye have not obeyed my voice. The judgment came with a reason attached.

An angel of the Lord came and sat under an oak in Ophrah, while Gideon threshed wheat by the winepress to hide it from the Midianites; that is how hard the oppression sat on the land, that a man hid his own harvest to keep it. The angel greets him: the Lord is with thee, thou mighty man of valour. The Most High already saw the warrior in the man hiding wheat.

Gideon answers, oh my Lord, if the Lord be with us, why then is all this befallen us, and where be all his miracles which our fathers told us of? A lot of us ask that same question today when we watch our people judged in the streets over and over: if we be the chosen people, why does all of this happen to us?

The Lord commissions him: go in this thy might, and thou shalt save Israel from the hand of the Midianites; have not I sent thee? Gideon answers with his pedigree: my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house. That is a defeated mentality, and we all have to overcome it, because every one of us was called for a reason, to put a brick in for the kingdom.

The Lord promises, surely I will be with thee, and thou shalt smite the Midianites as one man. Gideon asks for a sign that it is really the Lord talking with him; the least in his father's house wanted to be sure he was not talking to himself.

Gideon brings a kid and unleavened cakes, and the angel touches the flesh and the cakes with the end of his staff; fire rises up out of the rock and consumes them, and the angel departs out of his sight, gone just like that. No lighter fluid existed on the earth; the angel made fire come out of the rock, because the angels are made out of that fire.

When Gideon perceived he had seen an angel of the Lord face to face, he feared death, but the Lord said, peace be unto thee; fear not: thou shalt not die. Gideon built an altar there and called it Jehovah-shalom, which is, the Lord is peace.

The same night the Lord tells him to throw down his own father's altar of Baal, cut down the grove by it, and build an altar unto the Lord in its place. Notice this: even before the split of the kingdom, the tribes that would become the northern kingdom were already dabbling with Baal, worshipping the Lord in some fashion while holding onto the idol.

In the morning the men of the city found the altar of Baal cast down, and when they inquired, they said, Gideon the son of Joash hath done this thing. He crept at night, but somebody was peeping out a window; he was doing the right thing and still got told on. The grove they worshipped was a carved tree stump, cut and shaped to look like a particular god; that is the idol Gideon cut down. The men demand his death, but Joash stands up for his son: will ye plead for Baal? If he be a god, let him plead for himself, because one hath cast down his altar. Obviously he is no god; he is an idol. So that day Gideon was named Jerubbaal, saying, let Baal plead against him.

The Midianites, the Amalekites, and the children of the east gathered and pitched in the valley of Jezreel, but the Spirit of the Lord came upon Gideon; he blew a trumpet, and Abiezer, Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali came up to meet him. Those tribes are warriors; do not get it twisted. You see how Zebulun and Naphtali, who are in the south Americas right now, get down: that warrior spirit is still in them, only right now it has turned on each other, and the Most High is going to correct it and turn it right again.

Gideon asks the fleece signs: dew on the fleece only with dry earth beside, and then the reverse, dew on all the ground with the fleece dry. The Lord commands the dew, the condensation that falls through the night, to land exactly where he pleases; God can do whatever he wants, infinite power.

The Lord tells Gideon the people with him are too many for him to give Midian into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against him, saying, mine own hand hath saved me. That is Israel: look at what I did. The Lord knows how we think.

The people are yet too many; the Lord tries them at the water. Some lapped the water with their hand to their mouth as a dog lappeth, and all the rest bowed down upon their knees to drink; the lappers were three hundred men. What can we learn from this? You have to be willing to let go of some people. The Lord said, of whom I say, this shall not go with thee, the same shall not go: some people are not going to be beneficial to the war ahead of you, and the Lord will move them out of the way, but you have to be ready to let them go.

By the three hundred men that lapped will I save you, and deliver the Midianites into thine hand. The Lord sent the rest of Israel every man unto his tent and retained the three hundred, with victuals and trumpets in their hands. Now you know where the famous story of the three hundred came from: they got it from our ancestors, from Gideon. The nations take our history and make it entertainment, and even the artwork drew those three hundred with locks and braids and gave the other host the same, because the artist knew whose history he was drawing; those three hundred were Israelites.

The same night the Lord sends Gideon down to the outside of the enemy host with Phurah his servant: thou shalt hear what they say, and afterward shall thine hands be strengthened. There he hears a man telling his fellow a dream of a cake of barley bread tumbling into the host and overturning a tent, and his fellow interprets it: this is nothing else save the sword of Gideon, for into his hand hath God delivered Midian. The Lord put that dream into the mind of the enemy and sent Gideon down to hear it, so he could go into the battle valiant and strong, without any doubt. When Gideon heard the dream and the interpretation, he worshipped, and returned to say, arise; for the Lord hath delivered into your hand the host of Midian.

Gideon divides the three hundred into three companies, a hundred to the left flank, a hundred down the middle, a hundred to the right, and puts a trumpet in every man's hand, with empty pitchers and lamps within the pitchers. Look on me, and do likewise: pay attention, and when I blow the trumpet, blow ye also on every side of the camp, and say, the sword of the Lord, and of Gideon.

Gideon and his hundred come to the outside of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch, when they had but newly set the watch; in war you always have watchmen taking first, second, and third watch, and Gideon struck right in between the changing of the watchmen. The three companies blew the trumpets, brake the pitchers, held the lamps in their left hands and the trumpets in their right, and cried, the sword of the Lord, and of Gideon; and every man stood in his place round about the camp. Three hundred against thousands, you have to do something to mess with their mind: those horns blowing in unison put fear in the nations, and all the host ran, and cried, and fled. And the Lord set every man's sword against his fellow, even throughout all the host. The enemy destroyed itself; that is the Lord fighting the battle.

The men of Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh gathered themselves and pursued after the Midianites, and Gideon sent messengers throughout all mount Ephraim to come down and take the waters before them; and Ephraim took two princes of Midian, slaying Oreb upon the rock Oreb and Zeeb at the winepress of Zeeb. Ephraim, stand up; get this spirit back and come join your brothers in the war, because Judah is calling you right now. For those that may not know, that is you so-called Hispanics, you Puerto Ricans: you are Ephraim.

The men of Ephraim chode with Gideon sharply: why hast thou served us thus, that thou calledst us not when thou wentest to fight with the Midianites? Ephraim has an attitude because they got called late to the battle and wanted in from the beginning. Gideon answers with wisdom: is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer? God delivered into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb; what was I able to do in comparison of you? He gave them the best possible situation, the enemy fed right into their hands with nowhere to go, and then their anger was abated toward him.

Gideon and the three hundred pass over Jordan, faint, yet pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna the kings of Midian. He asks the men of Succoth for loaves of bread for his men, and the princes of Succoth answer, are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thine army? They try to play neutral ground for fear the kings might come against them if they helped. Gideon promises Succoth that when the Lord has delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into his hand, he will tear their flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers; and when the men of Penuel answer him the same way, he promises to break down their tower when he comes again in peace.

Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with about fifteen thousand men, all that were left of the host of the children of the east, for there fell an hundred and twenty thousand men that drew sword. Three hundred against those numbers: you know God was with them. Gideon went up by the way of them that dwelt in tents and smote the host while it was secure, and when the two kings fled, he pursued and took them, and discomfited all the host.

Returning from battle, Gideon caught a young man of Succoth who described unto him the princes and elders of the city, and he came back to Succoth with Zebah and Zalmunna in hand: behold the kings with whom ye did upbraid me. Gideon and his men had finished off Midian on an empty stomach because of them. He took the elders of the city, and thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he taught the men of Succoth; he taught them a lesson, that when the army of the Lord comes through faint and weary and asks for bread, you do not turn them away. And he beat down the tower of Penuel and slew the men of the city.

Zebah and Zalmunna describe the men they slew at Tabor: each one resembled the children of a king. Those were powerful men, and they were Gideon's brethren, the sons of his mother; as the Lord liveth, if ye had saved them alive, I would not slay you. Gideon tells Jether his firstborn, up, and slay them, but the youth drew not his sword, for he feared, because he was yet a youth. We have all had that moment of getting the nudge from pops and being nervous; the son was young, and that is understandable, but you see Gideon being a father, taking his son to the war and teaching him the ways he must walk.

The men of Israel ask Gideon to rule over them, both he, his son, and his son's son, for delivering them from the hand of Midian. Israel has always needed a leader, because we are lost sheep; we need somebody to guide us in the way we must go, or we wander off the path of righteousness. It has always been that way, and you see it playing out right here. Gideon refuses: I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you; the Lord shall rule over you.

Gideon requests of every man the earrings of his prey, for the enemy had golden earrings because they were Ishmaelites; and they willingly gave them, a thousand and seven hundred shekels of gold, beside the ornaments, collars, purple raiment, and camel chains of the kings. Gideon made an ephod thereof and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it, which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house.

Thus was Midian subdued before the children of Israel, so that they lifted up their heads no more, and the country was in quietness forty years in the days of Gideon. Gideon had threescore and ten sons, for he had many wives, and his concubine in Shechem bare him a son whose name he called Abimelech; and Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age. The sum of the history of Gideon, who is also named Jerubbaal, is this: the victory does not come in the strength of numbers, in how many guns or how many bullets you have. The victory of battle comes from the Lord, and that is why we have to trust in the Lord with all our heart and endure to the end, keeping these commandments until the return of our King of kings.

It came to pass, as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim, and made Baal-berith their god, and remembered not the Lord their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side; neither shewed they kindness to the house of Jerubbaal. The same cycle turns again the moment the judge is gone. That is the whole lesson of the book: our deliverance is never our own hand, and our downfall is always our own forgetting. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

When thou goest out to battle and seest horses and chariots and a people more than thou, be not afraid, for the Lord thy God is with thee, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt. That goes for us now, because we are still in a battle. We are not physically out battling the nations as our forefathers were when they took the land; we are in a spiritual battle, for the nations are confederate against Israel being a nation any more and against our remembrance of Israel and our laws. This whole world is set up for our people to go into sin and iniquity. Fear makes people trim their ways: afraid of family at the pagan holiday table, tucking their fringes in certain places, scared to be seen in the truth. Stand boldly; the Lord has not given us the spirit of fear, for that spirit came from Satan himself.

When Israel came nigh unto the battle, the priest approached and spoke: let not your hearts faint, fear not, do not tremble, neither be ye terrified, for the Lord your God is he that goeth with you to fight for you against your enemies to save you. A lot of times you do not see that the Lord is fighting for you in the spirit; that is where faith comes in, for the Bible is a faith-based book. You have to have faith that the Most High is fighting for you, with angels encamped round about the righteous, as David told us.

The officers sent home the man that had built a new house and not dedicated it, the man that had planted a vineyard and not eaten of it, and the man that had betrothed a wife and not taken her, lest he die in the battle and another man take his portion. You could very well die fighting for your people, so go enjoy these things first: dedicate your new house unto the Lord, eat the fruits of your labour from your vineyard, take your wife, then come to war for your people.

The fearful and fainthearted man was also sent home, lest his brethren's heart faint as well as his heart. The spirit of fear spreads: one man's fear makes the next man wonder what he knows, and soon the whole company questions the battle.

When the officers finished speaking, they made captains of the armies to lead the people, because you cannot have order without a ranking structure. Everybody cannot be calling the shots; there is one shot caller and the people follow, and that same order set in Moses' time is why a body under rank is proficient in everything it does.

When thou comest nigh unto a city to fight against it, first proclaim peace unto it. If it answered peace and opened, all the people found in it became tributaries unto Israel and served them. In this time Israel had the power to make nations tributaries. Right now we are not even a nation, just a people with Bibles and nothing established; but wait until Christ comes, for Israel will be established as a nation again and rule the earth, and the nations will be tributaries.

Israel came to a land with terms: agree, pay the tribute, and there is peace. If the city would make no peace but made war, Israel besieged it, and when the Lord delivered it into their hands, every male was smitten with the edge of the sword. The women, the little ones, the cattle, and all the spoil of the city Israel took unto themselves and ate the spoil of their enemies which the Lord their God had given them.

That was the rule for the cities very far off. But of the cities of the nations given Israel for an inheritance, thou shalt save alive nothing that breatheth; everything had to die, from humans to animals. The Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites were to be utterly destroyed for a stated purpose: that they teach you not to do after all their abominations which they have done unto their gods, their whoredoms, their idolatry, and their wicked ways of living, so that Israel sin not against the Lord.

In a long siege the trees for meat were not to be destroyed by forcing an axe against them, for thou mayest eat of them; the tree of the field is man's life. Only the trees known not to be trees for meat could be cut down to build bulwarks against the city that maketh war with thee, until it be subdued.

text.text: And there came an angel of the Lord, and sat under an oak which was in Ophrah, that pertained unto Joash the Abi–ezrite: and his son Gideon threshed wheat by the winepress, to hide it from the Midianites.
And the angel of the Lord appeared unto him, and said unto him, The Lord is with thee, thou mighty man of valour.

And Gideon said unto him, Oh my Lord, if the Lord be with us, why then is all this befallen us? and where be all his miracles which our fathers told us of, saying, Did not the Lord bring us up from Egypt? but now the Lord hath forsaken us, and delivered us into the hands of the Midianites.
And the Lord looked upon him, and said, Go in this thy might, and thou shalt save Israel from the hand of the Midianites: have not I sent thee?
And he said unto him, Oh my Lord, wherewith shall I save Israel? behold, my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house.
And the Lord said unto him, Surely I will be with thee, and thou shalt smite the Midianites as one man.

And it came to pass the same night, that the Lord said unto him, Take thy father’s young bullock, even the second bullock of seven years old, and throw down the altar of Baal that thy father hath, and cut down the grove that is by it:

And build an altar unto the Lord thy God upon the top of this rock, in the ordered place, and take the second bullock, and offer a burnt sacrifice with the wood of the grove which thou shalt cut down.

Then Gideon took ten men of his servants, and did as the Lord had said unto him: and so it was, because he feared his father’s household, and the men of the city, that he could not do it by day, that he did it by night.

And when the men of the city arose early in the morning, behold, the altar of Baal was cast down, and the grove was cut down that was by it, and the second bullock was offered upon the altar that was built.
And the Lord said unto Gideon, The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me.

Now therefore go to, proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, Whosoever is fearful and afraid, let him return and depart early from mount Gilead. And there returned of the people twenty and two thousand; and there remained ten thousand.

And the Lord said unto Gideon, The people are yet too many; bring them down unto the water, and I will try them for thee there: and it shall be, that of whom I say unto thee, This shall go with thee, the same shall go with thee; and of whomsoever I say unto thee, This shall not go with thee, the same shall not go.

So he brought down the people unto the water: and the Lord said unto Gideon, Every one that lappeth of the water with his tongue, as a dog lappeth, him shalt thou set by himself; likewise every one that boweth down upon his knees to drink.
And the number of them that lapped, putting their hand to their mouth, were three hundred men: but all the rest of the people bowed down upon their knees to drink water.
And the Lord said unto Gideon, By the three hundred men that lapped will I save you, and deliver the Midianites into thine hand: and let all the other people go every man unto his place.

So the people took victuals in their hand, and their trumpets: and he sent all the rest of Israel every man unto his tent, and retained those three hundred men: and the host of Midian was beneath him in the valley.
And he divided the three hundred men into three companies, and he put a trumpet in every man’s hand, with empty pitchers, and lamps within the pitchers.
And he said unto them, Look on me, and do likewise: and, behold, when I come to the outside of the camp, it shall be that, as I do, so shall ye do.
When I blow with a trumpet, I and all that are with me, then blow ye the trumpets also on every side of all the camp, and say, The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon.

So Gideon, and the hundred men that were with him, came unto the outside of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch; and they had but newly set the watch: and they blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers that were in their hands.

And the three companies blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers, and held the lamps in their left hands, and the trumpets in their right hands to blow withal: and they cried, The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon.
And they stood every man in his place round about the camp: and all the host ran, and cried, and fled.

And the three hundred blew the trumpets, and the Lord set every man’s sword against his fellow, even throughout all the host: and the host fled to Beth–shittah in Zererath, and to the border of Abel–meholah, unto Tabbath.
Thus was Midian subdued before the children of Israel, so that they lifted up their heads no more. And the country was in quietness forty years in the days of Gideon.
And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets:
Who through faith subdued kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions,
Quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.

When thou goest out to battle against thine enemies, and seest horses, and chariots, and a people more than thou, be not afraid of them: for the Lord thy God is with thee, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.
And it shall be, when ye are come nigh unto the battle, that the priest shall approach and speak unto the people,
And shall say unto them, Hear, O Israel, ye approach this day unto battle against your enemies: let not your hearts faint, fear not, and do not tremble, neither be ye terrified because of them;
For the Lord your God is he that goeth with you, to fight for you against your enemies, to save you.
